description:
What happens when we create space for people to express themselves? Through a series of life-altering events, Ryan Jack Nicholas explores how music and compassion can save lives. He reveals why society's pressure to conform silences difference, the devastating mental health consequences of masking, and how listening—truly listening—to others can transform our world and prevent tragedy. Ryan Jack Nicholas, a music psychology PhD candidate, neurodiversity advocate, and Westpac Future Leader on a mission to share the life-saving power of musical self-expression with the world! 

His work blends lived experience and research to challenge pathologising narratives and create space for every voice to be heard; both in music and in life. description: In my talk, I will weave how my brain cancer diagnosis forced me to hit reset and helped me realize our approach to poverty also needs a reset. The idea of pathways into and out of poverty, which led to the broken ladders idea, came from my realization that my medical team had never outlined a path for me to make it possible to be a long-term brain cancer survivor. Likewise, our country's poverty policy process and conversations don't outline any path that would make it possible to escape poverty/hunger, much less reach the goal of ending poverty and hunger for all. The way we've been going about it for the last 50 years, we will NEVER get there. We have to hit refresh and build pathways that make it possible for ALL people who work (and those who can't work) to meet their basic needs. description: Adam Rechnitz’s talk “Why We Drink Beer” blends brewer’s confession and cultural reflection. Beer, he argues, is not a villain or a lesser drink, but a deeply human way of savoring hard days, local ingredients, and being together. Adam Rechnitz helped start the craft brewing industry in NJ after a stint as a pioneer brewer in Seattle. A philosophy major and patron of the arts, he serves on the Trustee Board of Two River Theater, and hosts jazz, original music, original content and TEDxAsburyPark at Triumph Brewing. description: Hanna Garth’s “To Feast is Human” argues that sharing food is a fundamental way we become ourselves together. Drawing on stories from Cuba and beyond, she shows how marginalized families fight for “decent meals” amid scarcity, how feasts express care, identity, and belonging, and why food justice is inseparable from racial and economic justice—challenging us to see every table as a site of power and possibility Hanna Garth is a sociocultural and medical anthropologist at Princeton University whose research centers on food, inequality, race, and social justice. Author of “Food in Cuba: The Pursuit of a Decent Meal,” she examines how marginalized communities navigate structural barriers to accessing decent, nourishing food. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
